Whenever I've tried to learn about LLMs, machine learning, etc. I always come out with a bad feeling, compared to learning about software.
Theoretical courses make me feel like it's all baby steps, unless you assume a level of commitment equivalent to a math degree. could

comments.author: libraryofbabel

for

useful

But that's not the point; the point is understanding these things better by seeing how they are
made
(or
grown

do
deal with. This is one reason why
Crafting Interpreters
is such a beloved book here on HN.
LLMs are now at the core of tools we all use everyday... don't you want to know how they are made? comments.text: This article just explained the behaviour I’ve been seeing in my grandfather. He has dementia and used to hunt wild boar (very common in central Italy), but he knew the local wildlife well. Since developing dementia, for obvious reasons, he unfortunately hasn’t been the same. But a group of doves has nested on the gazebo on his terrace, and every year they come back (either them or their offspring). comments.author: rurp
comments.text:
Bird watching is something that my younger self would have never ever believed would be appealing, but it's actually really enjoyable! Getting out and exploring the natural world is great and I highly recommend it, but even for people without the opportunity or inclination to get out there birding is still extremely accessible.
Everyone can see birds around their home or work. Getting started can be as simple as noticing which birds you see regularly and figuring out what kind they are, and how the males and females differ in appearance (or don't). Usually males are the prettier more colorful ones, which is an effective signal for fitness.
Common birds will be easy to identify. Figuring out unusual birds or behaviors can turn into quite the detective project.
From there you can start to recognize calls and behavioral patterns. Once you learn a little bit in those areas it can be like seeing in another dimension. It's neat to hear a particular call and immediately know that there is a hawk in a nearby tree, or a cat behind a car.

comments.author: cmrx64
comments.text:
I’m an avid but amateur birdwatcher since some mental health struggles some years ago. I would go on long walks and eventually all these damn birds punctured my rumination and I tried making bird noises and they made bird noises back (I later learned these were Grackles, and they had arrived as a group to one of their preferred haunts). Once I started paying attention and interacting with more birds I got hooked.
It really is a very different cognitive mode. And when LLMs later came out I took my birdwatching-stance into it, which felt like a natural way to encounter some new entities.
I find it easy to believe that birdwatching is fairly distinctive in how it organizes the brain. Many sibling comments were wondering “is it the bird watching or is it an isolatable factor.” Bird watching is an extremely distinctive sensory integration, prediction, classification, etc task with lots of subproblems yes but also binding them in an irreducible way with agency detection (a vital part of cognition that modern environments are impoverished of) and attention.

stories.title_en: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM

comments.author: mmastrac
comments.text:
Amusingly constrained decoding is the same approach we use to turn an AR model into a /v1/systemone endpoint (I worked on the vLLM feature).
Tool calling is fraught with peril, especially because there's nothing that necessarily says that a models tools are fixed in place for the life of its run.
In some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss and (at least last time I checked!), the industry has not settled on OpenAI-style chat message formats for tool call updates.
I would absolutely prefer to run in a fully-constrained tool call environment, and would love if we hadn't YOLO'd the whole thing! The PTC-style tools sort of fix this by punting tool calling to JavaScript, but that's even harder to enforce, and models not trained on the style might take a turn of failed tool calls to get it right.

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text:
Constrained decoding has been in vLLM for a long time, and constrained tool call decoding has been in vLLM for a while, too.
The blog post is rather confusing because until you understand the entire situation it appears to imply that they fixed vLLM (what the title implies) but really they just needed to configure it correctly.
To be fair, the course of constrained tool calling configuration in vLLM changed over time in ways that changed behavior, which is the real problem. The Ubicloud team deserves a lot of credit for having benchmarks in place to track performance and catch regressions for investigations. Some of the providers you find on OpenRouter have inexplicably bad performance relative to others and clearly do not care this much.
However, if this article left you confused because constrained decoding and constrained tool call schema have been features in vLLM for a long time, jump to the end where they show what configuration changes they made.

comments.author: hansvm
comments.text: I wish they'd published something about the actual impact on model quality. Schema-constrained decoding changes the distribution the LLM will output. I'd be curious how a back-up-and-retry method for tool calls (which also doesn't pollute the context and also has 100% tool-call accuracy) would compare. In their example stats (23/25 success rate), it'd be +9% tokens used for the tool call attempt itself, but that's +9% on just a small fraction of the total tokens, so if a retry solution gave any better accuracy I think it might win out.

>  For example, when we served Kimi K2.6 with vLLM version 0.28, we got the expected tool call schema only 92% of the time. In other words, 2 out of every 25 attempted tool calls failed.
100% success is critical for tool calling.
The probability that the overall agent iteration is successful would scale very poorly even if we achieved 95%. With p95, if you need 50 tool calls that must execute sequentially to achieve a result, the chances that you
won't
have an error are only ~8%. There are ways to recover from bad tool calls (error feedback helps a lot), but if the agent is persistently using the wrong tools with the wrong args the overall system will not work very well.

stories.title_en: Websites Should Be Printable

comments.author: rkagerer
comments.text:
If a browser can show it on a screen, in fact screens of many sizes, it should be able to render to a printer.  With perfect fidelity.  It frustrates me to no end this isn't the case.
I posit the reason it sucks is because the Chrome team doesn't care (at least not enough) about the print feature.  Firefox is a little better.  But I haven't seen decent printing since the days of Internet Explorer.
Some of the most annoying culprits are website terms of service where printing to PDF produces page breaks in places that cut off lines of text.

comments.author: beej71
comments.text:
While I'm on board with having good html structure that prints well, and I'm on board with hiding navigation elements, etc., I'm not so on board with changing the default font size or fonts in the print version.
I just made a simple site that didn't set any font sizes anywhere, and a friend of mine complained that the font was too small on mobile. Do I detect a lo-res screen and increase the font size?
I know a lot of sites do exactly that, but I feel it's wrong. The user controls their default font size on their platform. What if they'd already increased it, and now I'm just making it bigger?
What if they'd decreased their default print font size and then I shrink it again?
I think it's best to leave those to the user entirely.

comments.author: pidgeon_lover
comments.text:
I agree that websites should be printable. I'm a fan of RSS and eInk displays (Kindles, and when I can afford one, a PC monitor), and printable websites would make using them on paper-like displays easier.
I've been using the PrintFriendly [1] browser extension for years (to print otherwise unprintable websites), but it gotten worse, so while looking at alternatives I started with The Printliminator [2] (which uses the Haartija CSS framework [3]) and have currently ended up using CopyAsMarkdown [4] (with Pandoc) and WebToEpub [5]
[1]
https://www.printfriendly.com/
[2]
https://github.com/CSS-Tricks/The-Printliminator
[3]
https://github.com/vladocar/Hartija---CSS-Print-Framework
[4]
https://github.com/yorkxin/copy-as-markdown/
[5]
https://github.com/dteviot/WebToEpub

comments.author: armcat
comments.text:
I politely disagree. The original intent Tim Berners Lee had [1] was to create a navigable way of finding documents and information. Not printable. The entire issue we have today is that we have blurred both the navigable and the printable concepts. A website should just be a simple clean space for easily navigating and conveying intended information. To print, we have latex and other markup methods that are perfect for that.

https://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html

comments.author: jillesvangurp

Debugging css issues related to print can be a bit of a PITA. Adding print options for dynamic content in a full stack page is not technically that hard. But getting it looking right can be a bit fussy. If you don't care about what things look like once printed, it's easy. But if you do care, it actually needs a bit of consideration.
I've done a few custom things with an application that generates labels for a label printer using just css and javascript. This is not that hard. But it does involve dealing with a lot of weirdness related to native print dialogs, vs. browser specific print dialogs (and their print previews), feature interaction with native printer settings and their scaling options, browsers adding footers to the printed document, and just general weirdness related to layout issues, page sizes, margins, etc.
My general feeling dealing with this is that CSS for print just gets a lot less scrutiny than regular CSS by browser developers.
